title: Learning Latin at Sixty-Seven
script: Narrator: [dry] At sixty-seven, I have taken up Latin, a decision my children regard with the bemused tenderness usually reserved for an elderly relative adopting an unusually demanding hobby.
Narrator: [wry] They are not entirely wrong to be bemused. I decline nouns at the kitchen table with the fierce concentration I once reserved for tax returns and considerably less success.

Narrator: [reflective] I retired eighteen months ago from a career spent, rather ironically, telling other people what to prioritize, and discovered almost immediately that I had no idea what I actually wanted for myself.

Narrator: [honest] Latin, of all things, was not an obvious answer. It offers no professional advantage at this stage, no credential worth the name, nothing but the private, faintly absurd satisfaction of finally parsing a sentence that resisted me the week before.
Narrator: [thoughtful] What nobody tells you about learning something difficult late in life is how thoroughly it dismantles the flattering myths you've accumulated about your own intelligence.

Narrator: [candid] I was, by most measures, a competent professional for four decades, and none of that competence transfers even slightly to memorizing the ablative case at an age when memory itself has become unreliably generous.

Narrator: [wry] My grandson, eleven years old and insufferably pleased with himself, now corrects my declensions over dinner, and I have decided to find this charming rather than mortifying, a decision that requires renewed effort roughly twice a week.
Narrator: [warmly] There is something clarifying about being a genuine beginner again, stripped of the accumulated authority that made me, for years, reluctant to ask an obvious question aloud.

Narrator: [reflective] I no longer confuse difficulty with unsuitability, a distinction that eluded me for most of my working life, when struggle felt like proof I'd chosen wrongly rather than proof I was actually learning.

Narrator: [resolved] I doubt I'll ever read Virgil unaided, and I've stopped pretending that's the point. The point, apparently, was always the humbling, unglamorous pleasure of being thoroughly, cheerfully bad at something new.

quiz.question: What does learning Latin late in life dismantle, according to the narrator?
options: The flattering myths she had accumulated about her own intelligence
quiz.explanation: She says it thoroughly dismantles the flattering myths accumulated about one's own intelligence.

The distinction between difficulty and unsuitability
